 Election Day checklist: Everything you need before hitting the polls
 The Boys and Girls Club of Bloomington is pictured Oct. 20, 2026, in Bloomington. The space continues to serve as a polling place in the upcoming election season.
 Photo by Kaitlyn Stacy 
 / The Indiana Daily Student
 By
 Lily Saylor 
 Oct 21, 2026 5:14 pm 
 · Updated Oct 21, 2026 5:14 pm 
 In less than two weeks, it will be Nov. 3: Election Day.  Here’s a comprehensive guide on what to check to ensure you are prepared to vote at the polls.     
 Registration   
 First, you must be registered to vote. Oct. 5 was the last day for Hoosiers to register, but you can check your voter registration status online at Indiana Voters . You must be registered to vote in the county you are voting in. You can use the Monroe County Voter Information Map to check what precinct you are voting in.   
 Location     
 Polls are open from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m. on Election Day. To find the correct polling location, visit Indiana 's Voter Portal   and select “Find Your Polling Place.” From there, you can search for a polling location by voter registration, county, precinct or split precinct.   
 Students can vote on campus at the Indiana Memorial Union. For more information, check this  guide to polling locations .  Indiana University students living in Bloomington precincts 5, 18, 19 and 23 can vote at the IMU, according to a 2024 X post from IU Bloomington.   
 Identification   
 At the polls, you must provide a valid form of identification. This includes an Indiana driver’s license, a U.S. passport, Indiana State Identification Card or Military ID card. Your photo ID must meet four criteria : it must display your photo and name, have an expiration date and be issued by the State of Indiana or the U.S. government.   
 College students may register at either the address where they attend school , or their home address. You cannot use an out-of-state license to vote in Monroe County; you may obtain a free identification card for voting purposes at the Bureau of Motor Vehicles.    
 First-time Indiana voters may be required to present proof of residency documentation before voting to confirm their Indiana residence address.   
 If your ID expired after the last general election — Nov. 5, 2024 — it is still a valid form of identification for this year’s election.    
 If you do not currently have a photo ID, you can obtain a free state-issued ID at the BMV. The Bloomington BMV Branch is located at 1531 S. Curry Pike Ste. 500. The Branch is open 9 a.m. to 6:30 p.m. Tuesday, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Wednesday through Friday and 9 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. Saturday.    
 If you do not have identification, or if a member of the precinct election board determines your ID does not qualify under state law, you may be required to cast a provisional ballot .    
 An ID may be challenged if you are unable or unwilling to present photo ID that meets the requirements, if you are not a U.S. citizen or if you will be under the age of 18 by Nov. 5. You may also be challenged if your name does not appear on the poll list or if you do not currently reside in the precinct you are voting in.    
 To cast a provisional ballot, you must mark the ballot privately, unless you request and are entitled to assistance. Provisional ballots are also cast on a traditional hand-counted ballot or an optical scan ballot card, as opposed to the direct record electronic voting system, and they are kept separate from other cast ballots. After Election Day, the county election board will determine if your ballot should be counted.   
 If you cast a provisional ballot, you have until noon 10 days after the election to find out if your ballot was counted. If your ballot is not counted, you will be provided with the reason why by contacting the county election board or checking the voter portal if you are registered to vote in the county that you cast your provisional vote in.   
 Student IDs will not be accepted as a valid form of identification this election. Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita said in an X post in April that Senate Bill 10 is a “commonsense protection” to “prevent potential fraud.”   
 A Women4Change spokesperson told the IDS in April that the bill banning student IDs as a form of identification is “likely unconstitutional.” Isaac Chapman-Whitehead, president of IU’s chapter of College Democrats, also told the IDS in April that banning student IDs to vote will turn a lot of students away from the polls.    
 For more information about Election Day, visit The Indiana Voter Portal .
